newsitem.title: UK: Indium shortage in minor metals market, rest quiet.
newsitem.headline: Indium shortage in minor metals market, rest quiet.

text.p: Trading in industrial minor metals remained largely subdued this week, though indium chased higher on continued Japanese demand -- a condition that was showing few signs of slowing.
Elsewhere, cobalt bottomed out after recent downside pressure and looked to firm, while antimony continued to drift amid the lack of consumer enquiry.
"Generally the market is finding few fresh enquiries and most of the metals in the sector are holding around last weeks levels," one trader said.
Indium continued to target levels of $300 a kilo and possibly higher as Japanese consumers rushed to cover in a market largely devoid of good quality material.
Western producers were said to be running very low stocks.
Several traders suggested prices had the potential to hit $400 near-term.
"There is little flowing out of China and Western producers have been caught short in the wake of the demand from Japan," one European trader said.
The metal used in the electronics industry and in high performance bearings used in sports cars traded at $250 and $275 a kilo basis warehouse Rotterdam.
The recent sharp and sustained move in indium saw Indium Corp of America raise its price by $35 to $260 a kilo, the second such move recently.
Traders said this largely confirmed that the market was extremely tight. For around 15 months Indium Corp had consistently lowered prices.
Cobalt held steady levels after recent downside pressure, though upside progress was capped by producer sales.
Traders said the market had the potential to turn. "Prices have the ability to recover to higher levels over the next two months," one trader said."
War-torn Zaire failed to inspire any upside ticks in the cobalt market.
"Its been largely factored into prices," one London trader commented.
European traders said most of their attention focused on a U.S. DLA sale. The market is often pressured lower by traders around the time of DLA sales, they explained.
The Defense National Stockpile will announce the outcome of its sale of 1.1 million pounds of cobalt, offered on a negotiated bid basis, by mid-March.
The deadline for the bidding was February 20.

Traders suggested the quality of the material on offer was lower than usual, below 90 percent cobalt. On Wednesday the stockpile invited bids on a sealed basis for one million pounds of higher grade metals, 93 to 96 percent cobalt.
Antimony after the recent Chinese New Year drifted in lacklustre trade.
Traders said enquiries remained slow, though noted growing demand in the US.
Referring to the antimony market one trader said, "Consumers are holding off for lower numbers under the impression that the Chinese may turn sellers near-term," one London trader said.
Rhodium after a recent mauling from investment fund selling may be making a comeback, though several traders believed this would only be a temporary respite.
They believed that speculators may gain be tempted to rock the market on any signs of a significant recovery.
"Its going to head below $200 an ounce again soon," one trader said.
The spectre of sales of Russian stockpiled metals waned over the past week, traders said.

Recently traders said they believed that 420 tonnes of cobalt, 30,000 76 Ib flasks of mercury, 7,000 tonnes of titanium sponge and an undisclosed amount of chrome could be released from strategic stockpiles.
Referring to titanium one source said the levels involved were more likely to be around 1,000 tonnes. "After the metal has been reprocessed it will be used in the internal market," the source said.
"Little or any is likely to find its way out of Russia."
Over production kept the magnesium market on a back footing, while molybdenum after recent gains eased under profit-taking.
Silicon lumps remained well supported against the backdrop of EU anti-dumping duties.
Silicon is consumed in the aluminium industry where it is used to make aluminium alloys.
